title: Hollis Bay Snacks New Product Launch
prompt: Our client is Hollis Bay Snacks, a regional US snack company best known for its kettle-cooked potato chips. Hollis Bay sells about $300 million a year through grocery stores and mass retailers in the Northeast and Midwest. Chip sales have been flat for several years, while “better-for-you” snacks are growing quickly. Hollis Bay has developed a line of roasted chickpea snacks — crunchy, high in protein and lower in fat than chips — and is deciding whether to launch them next spring. The board will approve the launch only if it breaks even in its first year. The CEO has asked us whether Hollis Bay should launch, and what it should do to make the launch a success.
interviewerNotes: Source: AI Casing Case 07 (v1.0, Oct 2026), interviewer-led mode; main skill is creativity — protect at least 3 minutes for the brainstorm. Break-even: contribution per bag = $3.00 − ($0.70 + $0.30 + $0.30 + $0.20) = $1.50; first-year launch costs = $3.0M + $4.5M + $1.5M = $9.0M (the $1.2M of recipe development is already spent and doesn't count); break-even = 6.0 million bags. Demand: (10% × 60%) + (20% × 20%) = 10% of 30M households = 3.0M buying households × 3 bags = 9.0M bags — 1.5× break-even, ≈ $4.5M profit. Risk: repeat buying — break-even needs 2 bags per buying household, and 45% aren't sure they'd like the taste (70% like it in blind tests). Sampling: 500,000 extra households × 3 bags × $1.50 = $2.25M − $1.5M = +$0.75M (break-even 1.0M bags). Recommendation: launch, built around trial — sampling, promotion on Hollis Bay's own chip bags, a 'high protein, less fat' message. Release order in the guide: Exhibits 1 (bag economics) and 2 (shopper survey) in either order; Exhibit 3 (sampling proposal) only in the brainstorm module, after both, when the candidate proposes sampling or after their ideas.

dataLedger.label: The product
dataLedger.value: The product is roasted chickpea snacks in 5-ounce bags, launching in three flavors, with about twice the protein of chips and less fat.

dataLedger.label: Where it would be sold
dataLedger.value: The new line is for the same grocery and mass-retail stores that carry Hollis Bay chips.

dataLedger.label: Manufacturing
dataLedger.value: Chickpeas can't run on the chip fryers, so Hollis Bay would lease a new roasting line, which is about six months from being ready.

dataLedger.label: What "break even in year one" means
dataLedger.value: Breaking even in year one means first-year profit from the new line, after its own costs, has to be zero or better.

dataLedger.label: Why now
dataLedger.value: Chip sales are flat, better-for-you snacks are growing quickly, and Hollis Bay's largest retailers have asked for healthier options.

dataLedger.label: Competition in general
dataLedger.value: Several small better-for-you brands are selling roasted chickpea snacks, and no large national brand is dominant in this kind of snack in Hollis Bay's stores.

dataLedger.label: Hollis Bay's goals beyond year one
dataLedger.value: Hollis Bay's hope is that the line becomes a growth platform for more better-for-you snacks.

dataLedger.label: Price Hollis Bay receives per bag (and the shelf price)
dataLedger.value: The price Hollis Bay receives from retailers is $3.00 per 5-ounce bag; shoppers would pay about $3.99 in stores, and retailers keep the difference.

dataLedger.label: Variable costs per bag: ingredients, packaging, roasting, freight
dataLedger.value: Variable costs per bag are $0.70 for ingredients, $0.30 for packaging, $0.30 for roasting labor and energy, and $0.20 for freight to retailers, and they rise with every bag made.

dataLedger.label: First-year launch costs: roasting line, marketing, shelf fees
dataLedger.value: First-year launch costs are $3.0 million for the new roasting line (lease and staff), $4.5 million for marketing and advertising, and $1.5 million in shelf fees paid to retailers to stock the new line.

dataLedger.label: Recipe development (already spent)
dataLedger.value: Recipe development was $1.2 million, already spent last year.

dataLedger.label: Survey: purchase intent at $3.99
dataLedger.value: Asked how likely they are to buy at $3.99 a bag, 10% of shoppers said definitely, 20% probably, 30% might or might not, 25% probably not and 15% definitely not.

dataLedger.label: Survey: what shoppers like most
dataLedger.value: What shoppers like most is high protein (52%), less fat than chips (40%), the crunch, like chips (31%), and being good for kids' lunches (18%).

dataLedger.label: Survey: what makes shoppers hesitate
dataLedger.value: The top hesitations are not being sure they'd like the taste (45%), the price being a bit high (22%), being happy with current snacks (20%), and not thinking of Hollis Bay for healthy snacks (12%).

dataLedger.label: Survey design
dataLedger.value: The survey is of 1,000 snack shoppers in Hollis Bay's region; each response represents one household, and in the like and hesitate questions shoppers could pick up to two answers.

dataLedger.label: Planning assumptions: households, conversion rates, bags per household
dataLedger.value: Planning assumptions from Hollis Bay's past launches are: 30 million households shop in stores carrying Hollis Bay; 60% of “definitely would buy” and 20% of “probably would buy” shoppers actually buy in year one, and none of the others do; and each buying household averages 3 bags in year one.

dataLedger.label: In-store sampling proposal: scope, cost, extra households, bags
dataLedger.value: The sampling proposal is staffed tasting tables in 500 stores over 10 weekends at launch, costing $1.5 million, and it is expected to bring 500,000 extra buying households in year one, each buying 3 bags, on top of the survey-based forecast; the cost is in addition to the launch costs.

dataLedger.label: Cannibalization of Hollis Bay chips
dataLedger.value: Fewer than 5% of chickpea-snack purchases are expected to replace a bag of Hollis Bay's own chips — small enough to ignore for this decision.

dataLedger.label: How reliable the survey is
dataLedger.value: The 1,000 shoppers are a match for the mix in Hollis Bay's stores, and the conversion rates are from Hollis Bay's last five launches.

dataLedger.label: Taste test results
dataLedger.value: In blind taste tests, 70% of people who tried the snack were positive, rating it good or very good.

dataLedger.label: Competitor prices
dataLedger.value: Competing roasted chickpea snacks are priced at $4.29–$4.99 per 5-ounce bag.

dataLedger.label: Retailer support
dataLedger.value: Hollis Bay's two largest retail partners have agreed to stock the line in all their stores, provided Hollis Bay pays the shelf fees.

exhibits.interpretationKey: Stated intent overstates buying: 30% say definitely or probably, but with past conversion rates (10% × 60%) + (20% × 20%) = 10% of 30M households buy = 3.0M × 3 bags = 9.0M bags, 1.5× break-even (≈ $4.5M profit). The forecast leans on repeat: each buying household must buy at least 2 bags — at one bag each Hollis Bay sells 3.0M and loses ~$4.5M — and the top hesitation is taste (45%). Lead with protein (52%) and lower fat (40%). Like/hesitate answers allow two picks, so they add to more than 100%.

exhibits.interpretationKey: 500,000 × 3 = 1.5 million extra bags × $1.50 = $2.25M of contribution − $1.5M cost = +$0.75M; it needs 1.0 million bags (~333,000 households) to pay for itself, so it still breaks even at two-thirds of the expected uplift. It attacks the biggest worry (45% unsure of the taste; 70% like it once they try it) and protects the 2-bag repeat threshold. Each bag contributes the same as in Exhibit 1.

structureKey: A strong structure turns 'should we launch, and how?' into prioritized questions: economics (price Hollis Bay receives, cost per bag, launch costs → break-even volume); customers and demand (who would buy, how many, how often; what they like or worry about); competition (better-for-you brands and their prices); and company fit (manufacturing, retailers, brand stretch from chips). Strong candidates use the board's rule to set the test (break-even volume vs. likely year-one volume), split demand into trial and repeat, ask about cannibalization of the chips, and flag that a chip brand may not read as healthy. Red flags: jumping to flavors and packaging with no economics, generic frameworks, ignoring repeat purchase.
recommendationKey: Yes — launch, with a plan built around getting shoppers to taste the product. Each bag earns $1.50 after variable costs and first-year launch costs are $9.0M (the $1.2M already spent on recipes doesn't count), so break-even is 6.0 million bags. The shopper survey points to about 3 million buying households × 3 bags = 9.0 million bags — 1.5× break-even and about $4.5M of first-year profit. The risk is repeat buying: break-even needs each buying household to buy at least 2 bags, and 45% of shoppers aren't sure they'd like the taste (70% like it once they try it). So the launch should push trial: in-store sampling pays for itself (+$0.75M), and Hollis Bay can promote the new snack on its own chip bags, with a 'high protein, less fat' message. Next steps: lock in shelf space with the two biggest retailers and track repeat purchases closely in the first three months.
